stories.headline: Seahawks' Quenton Nelson, Sam Darnold among starters ruled out
stories.summary: New Seahawks trade acquisition Quenton Nelson will have a "minor procedure" and is one of six starters, including QB Sam Darnold, who won't play vs. the Cardinals.
stories.body:
RENTON, Wash. -- One week after arriving via a trade, Seattle Seahawks All-Pro left guard Quenton Nelson needs a "minor procedure" on his knee, coach Mike Macdonald said Friday.

Sources told NFL Network's Ian Rapoport that Nelson's surgery will be to clean out cartilage in his knee.

Macdonald said Nelson will not go on injured reserve, and he'll be designated as week-to-week.

Nelson and quarterback Sam Darnold, who has a quad injury, are among six starters ruled out by the Seahawks (4-4) for Sunday's game against the Arizona Cardinals (3-5) at Lumen Field. The others are defensive tackle Leonard Williams (stinger), outside linebacker Uchenna Nwosu (ankle), left tackle Charles Cross (ankle) and wide receiver/returner Rashid Shaheed (knee).

While Nelson is out, Seattle will move Grey Zabel back to left guard and reinsert Anthony Bradford into the starting lineup at right guard. After acquiring Nelson from the Indianapolis Colts for a 2027 third-round pick and a 2028 fifth-round pick, the Seahawks moved Zabel to right guard, where Bradford had been their starter.

"He had something that he was dealing with when he got here and we re-imaged it and it was aggravated to some degree," Macdonald said of Nelson's injury. "We've kind of done the due diligence, and everybody agrees that it's best to take care of it now and play the long game. He'll be week-to-week at this point."

Nelson, 30, played every offensive snap in the Seahawks' loss to the Chicago Bears on Monday night. He was seen this week with a sleeve on his right leg, was listed as limited Wednesday and did not practice the past two days.

"I can't give you all the details on what it was and what we found," Macdonald said. "Obviously, he passed the physical, so I think two things are true: One, that it was something that he was dealing with coming out of whatever game it was before the trade, and I think it's been aggravated since he got here."

Darnold, who suffered a cracked rib on the second play of Monday's game and then injured his quad toward the end of the game, will not go on IR, Macdonald said.

Macdonald on Friday said Drew Lock will be the starter against the Cardinals, despite a right elbow injury that had him inactive the past two games and limited his throwing in recent weeks. He was again listed as a limited participant Friday, as he has been on all 12 injury reports released since the start of Week 6.

Macdonald said earlier in the week that the Seahawks had to also get Jalen Milroe, who has not appeared in a regular-season game since Week 5 of last year, ready to play in case they needed to turn to their third quarterback against Arizona. He said Friday that they've had to manage Lock's reps this week, which was "more precautionary than anything else."

After Darnold suffered a glute injury on the fifth play of the opener, Lock played most of the first two games, posting an 82.5 Total QBR that ranked sixth best in that span. Three of his four touchdown passes came in a win 31-7 win over the Cardinals in Week 2.

The Seahawks also added some quarterback insurance earlier this week by signing former United Football League MVP Adrian Martinez to their practice squad.

Cross, Shaheed and Nwosu all missed the Bears game, while Williams went down in the third quarter. The only one of the four who practiced at all this week was Nwosu, who was limited Wednesday.

Josh Jones will start again at left tackle for Cross.

Seattle also ruled out backup defensive tackle Brandon Pili (back) and lists backup outside linebacker Connor O'Toole (foot) as questionable.

stories.headline: Josh Norris scores twice in the Sabres' 5-2 victory over the Blue Jackets
stories.summary: — Josh Norris scored twice, defenseman Owen Power had three assists and the Buffalo Sabres beat the Columbus Blue Jackets 5-2 on Friday night.
stories.body:
BUFFALO, N.Y. -- — Josh Norris scored twice, defenseman Owen Power had three assists and the Buffalo Sabres beat the Columbus Blue Jackets 5-2 on Friday night.


Norris ended a six-game goals drought to help Buffalo win for the fourth time in five games.


Jack Quinn, Rasmus Dahlin and Josh Doan also scored, and Ukko-Pekka Luukkonen made 24 saves.


Kent Johnson and Zach Werenski scored for Columbus, and Jet Greaves made 32 saves. The Blue Jackets have lost three straight road games.


Quinn opened the scoring at 6:50 of the first period with his ninth of the season, and Johnson tied it with 4:00 left in the period with his eighth. Norris made it 2-1 with 1:50 to go in the first with his first goal since Oct. 17.


Dahlin made it 3-1 with a one-timer 4:30 into the second period. Norris’ second goal at 9:46 made it 4-1. Doan made it 5-1 1:07 later.


Werenski's power-play goal with 1:39 left in the third made it 5-2.


Blue Jackets forward Sean Monahan left the second period because of a lower-body injury and did not return. He blocked Dahlin's shot during his last shift.


Up next
Blue Jackets: Host Florida on Tuesday night.


Sabres: Host Vegas on Sunday.

stories.headline: Alexander-Walker’s 28 points lead Hawks past Wizards; Young scores 23 in return to Atlanta
stories.summary: — Nickeil Alexander-Walker scored 28 points and the Atlanta Hawks held off the Washington Wizards 139-132 in an NBA Cup game Friday night.
stories.body:
ATLANTA -- — Nickeil Alexander-Walker scored 28 points and the Atlanta Hawks held off the Washington Wizards 139-132 in an NBA Cup game Friday night.


It was the third straight win for the Hawks and second straight against the Wizards, as Atlanta swept the home-and-home series.


Trae Young had 23 points, 10 assists and a season-high eight turnovers in his first game in Atlanta as a visitor after being traded last season after seven-plus years with the Hawks.


Lu Dort had 25 points, including a crucial shot clock-beating corner jumper late in the fourth quarter. Onyeka Okongwu scored 22 points and Aaron Wiggins added 19 points off the bench for Atlanta. Dyson Daniels guarded Young for much of the game and finished with 13 points and 12 assists.


Kyshawn George scored 33 points for the Wizards, who were without Anthony Davis (sprained right ankle). Tre Johnson had 23 points, including five 3-pointers.


The Hawks pushed the pace the entire game, and their 139 points were a season-high. It was also the most points the Wizards have surrendered this season. The Hawks shot 53% (52 for 98) from the field and 42% (16 for 38) from 3-point range.


Washington stayed in the game with hot 3-point shooting, hitting 11 of its first 15 in the second half and ending the game at 53% (18 for 34).


Overall No. 1 draft pick AJ Dybantsa had 11 points on 3-for-13 shooting for Washington.


Hawks forward Jalen Johnson missed his third straight game with a left ankle sprain.


Up next
Wizards: At Oklahoma City on Saturday.


Hawks: Host the Brooklyn Nets on Saturday.

stories.headline: Witness: Clase 'inside' pitch info dried up amid Mizuhara case fallout
stories.summary: A witness said that the inside info he used to bet on Clase pitches dried up due to increased scrutiny from the scandal involving Shohei Ohtani's interpreter.
stories.body:
NEW YORK -- A government witness testified Friday in the federal trial of Cleveland Guardians pitchers Emmanuel Clase and Luis Ortiz that the inside information he used to bet regularly on Clase pitches in 2023 dried up the next season due to increased scrutiny from the gambling scandal involving Shohei Ohtani's interpreter at the time.

Luis de Aza Baez said he placed dozens of bets and won thousands of dollars by wagering on the velocity of select Clase pitches during the 2023 season, "because I had inside information." Clase is accused of conspiring with bettors to rig 18 pitches over three seasons.

De Aza Baez said that when he asked for more information on Clase pitches in 2024, he was told that because of "what was going on with Ohtani, there was no more information like that."

Ohtani, the Los Angeles Dodgers' superstar, came under scrutiny in March 2024 after ESPN reported that millions of dollars had been sent from his bank account to an illegal bookmaking operation. His longtime interpreter, Ippei Mizuhara, later pleaded guilty to stealing nearly $17 million from Ohtani to pay off gambling debts and is currently in prison. Ohtani was cleared of any wrongdoing.

De Aza Baez, who worked as an Uber driver, told prosecutors that he began receiving information about the pitches from Enoc Pena, an associate of Clase's, in 2023. De Aza Baez said the tips often came through a group chat titled "Uber Inc." that Pena started and included other men who have been referenced in the case and also worked for the ride-share company in Massachusetts at the time.

Prosecutors showed a screenshot of a text message Clase allegedly sent to Pena on Sept. 30, 2023, when the Guardians were scheduled to play the Detroit Tigers, that talked about "killing the first two chickens." De Aza Baez said the message was instructions to bet on a Clase pitch to the third batter of an inning, but only if Clase had retired the first two batters. Clase did not appear in the game.

Clase's defense has argued that mentions of roosters and chickens in such communications often were referencing cockfighting, a legal activity in the Dominican Republic, where Clase and others in the case are from.

De Aza Baez said he became friends with Pena as well as Robinson Vásquez Germosen and Luis Arismendy Paca Méndez, who are co-defendants in the case, while they were all living in Nantucket, Massachusetts. Paca Méndez, who has pleaded not guilty, is not participating in the trial after being extradited from the Dominican Republic to the U.S. on Oct. 19.

De Aza Baez said he met Clase when Vásquez and Pena brought the pitcher to his house for a birthday party on April 28, 2023, in Winthrop, Massachusetts, where De Aza Baez had moved. He met Clase again a few days later at a relative's house. Prosecutors showed a video of the gathering, with Clase playing dominoes on a table featuring a Boston Red Sox logo. The Guardians were in town for a series against the Red Sox.

De Aza Baez said he never received any information directly from Clase, only from Pena. De Aza Baez said he did not have an agreement with Pena but gave him money because he "almost always" won using the information to bet on Clase's pitches. De Aza Baez acknowledged opening a DraftKings betting account under his wife's name to increase the amount he could wager and win on his Clase bets. De Aza Baez also said he included the Clase pitch bets in parlays to maximize payouts.

De Aza Baez acknowledged that he had agreed with the government to forfeit $69,000 from his winning bets on Clase and would "tell the truth" in exchange for prosecutors dropping a wire fraud charge related to the case.

Clase, Ortiz and Vásquez have pleaded not guilty to conspiracy charges of wire and honest services fraud, sports bribery and money laundering.

"Our defense is the same today as it was in opening: This is a case about big talk and small bets," Vásquez's attorney Todd Spodek told ESPN after Friday's hearing. "We're confident leaving that judgment to the jury."

The trial will continue next Thursday in Brooklyn.

stories.headline: Wings' Paige Bueckers, Azzi Fudd talk relationship on pod
stories.summary: Azzi Fudd hosted Wings teammate Paige Bueckers on her podcast and the two discussed their relationship, Dallas' season and Fudd's recovery from knee surgery.
stories.body:
Dallas Wings teammates Azzi Fudd and Paige Bueckers, the past two WNBA No. 1 draft picks, spoke on Fudd's podcast Friday about a variety of topics, including a personal life update.

"We're not together anymore; it's been a while," Bueckers said on the "Fudd Around and Find Out" podcast. "[We] share that because everybody [was] like, 'Oh my gosh, they're teammates, how is this going to work?'"

Bueckers and Fudd, who were teammates in college at UConn, said they felt the need to address their relationship status in part because of allegations it factored into the Wings picking Fudd at No. 1 in April. Fudd was chosen over TCU guard Olivia Miles, who went on to be the Rookie of the Year for the Minnesota Lynx. Spain's Awa Fam (Seattle Storm) was taken third, followed by teammates from the 2026 champion UCLA Bruins: Lauren Betts (Washington Mystics), Gabriela Jaquez (Chicago Sky) and Kiki Rice (Toronto Tempo).

Fudd, Fam, Betts and Miles were all No. 1 at different points in ESPN's mock draft in the months before the April draft. Bueckers said her previous relationship with Fudd had no impact on Dallas' decision.

"We were not together before she got drafted," Bueckers said. "She was not drafted because she was my girlfriend. She was drafted because she deserved it. She's an amazing human, an amazing basketball player. And we're still friends, we're still cool.

"We played an entire season together; we're the utmost professionals."

Fudd averaged 13.1 points but was limited to just 30 games after an injury to her right knee led to season-ending arthroscopic surgery in August. She offered an update on her health.

"My offseason's been good," Fudd said. "Lots of rehab, lots of training, lots of on-court workouts, lots of traveling. It's been busy.

"I think there's a lot I can improve on. Especially the iso game; I feel like I'm not too comfortable with that yet. I know I'm capable of doing a little bit more. Watching someone like Paige who is able to create from anywhere ... that's great inspiration for me."

Bueckers averaged 20.9 points, 4.1 rebounds and 5.9 assists, and was named to the All-WNBA second team as Dallas reached the playoffs as the No. 7 seed.

The Wings were eliminated in the first round by the eventual champion Golden State Valkyries. Bueckers said she learned a lot from her first playoff experience and complimented Golden State.

"The Valkyries' defense, I can't explain to you how tough they are," Bueckers said. "They swarm, they send bodies, they trap you, they blitz you, they're so connected. I'm glad I got to have that experience against them to open my eyes to what the playoffs are like -- the physicality, the pressure, the environment.

"And I'm proud of our season. I hated losing; I sat and was pissed about it for like a week. I reached out to [Sue Bird] about it, what was her first playoff experience like. I didn't play as well as I wanted to. But it was my first experience, going against a really good opponent, and I was learning and growing through it all."

Fudd and Bueckers also addressed the Wings' move to the 19,000-seat American Airlines Center in downtown Dallas next season after playing at UT Arlington's College Park Center, which seats over 7,000, since the franchise relocated to Texas in 2016.

"UTA was a vibe; we had a ball, we did our thing there," Bueckers said. "But definitely excited to move into Dallas. New times."

While the change in venue will lead to more eyes on Wings games, the two players said they're hoping for less scrutiny of any on-court behavior.

Both said fans shouldn't read into interactions the two have with each other or their teammates as anything other than normal team behavior. They also said they don't stand for "hate of any kind" or "tearing people down to lift us up."

"We've seen a lot of negativity," Bueckers said. "We've had stuff sent to us, stuff sent to our family, our friends. There's been some crazy things said about us. We still support each other, we're still going to be great friends, we're still going to be great teammates. All the negative things can be put aside, and you don't need to overanalyze everything."

Fudd added with a chuckle, "Also, we don't need messages [from fans] on what the other person's doing. We've addressed everything we need to, and the rest will stay with us."

stories.headline: F1 to make a decision on season finale in Imola next week - sources
stories.summary: Formula 1 has a cut-off date next week to let Italian circuit Imola know whether it is needed to replace two Middle East races as the 2026 season finale.
stories.body:
Formula 1 has a cut-off date next week to let Italian circuit Imola know whether it is needed to replace two Middle East races as the 2026 season finale, sources told ESPN.

As it stands, Formula 1 will finish the year with a triple header of races in Las Vegas (Nov. 21), Qatar (Nov. 29) and Abu Dhabi (Dec. 6).

Those final two races are uncertain, given the U.S-Iran war and ongoing tensions in the region.

Imola is on stand-by to hold a race on Dec. 6 if hostilities in the Middle East escalate in the next few weeks and those last two events need to be cancelled, but the circuit has to know whether the event is taking place in the near future.

Teams ESPN have spoken to are working to an assumption that a decision will be made on Imola next week.

Asked about the situation after Friday practice in Brazil, Haas boss Aayo Komatsu appeared to confirm a deadline.

"I understand Tuesday [Nov. 10] Imola needs be told if we go to Imola or not," Komatsu told Sky Sports on Friday in Brazil.

Imola has already started work on constructing grandstands, with F1 footing the bill.

Sources within F1 have downplayed the idea to ESPN of a fixed date for a decision, as extensions can be given to Imola if F1 feel one is required, but it is clear Imola and the teams need to know before they go to Las Vegas whether that contingency plan still exists.

Sources have told ESPN that the date Komatsu said is broadly accurate and it seems unlikely a decision on Imola will be made much later than the end of next week.

Once the cut-off date is passed, Formula 1 is then in uncharted territory without a back-up option.

- Kimi Antonelli fastest in second practice at São Paulo GP as new world champion

- Ferrari confirms talks to diffuse Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc tension

- George Russell hit with five-place grid penalty for São Paulo Grand Prix

Should there be an escalation in hostilities after Imola has stopped preparing to host a race, it would be likely that F1's season ends with the Las Vegas Grand Prix.

Contractually, that hypothetical would nudge F1 into a tricky position, as the commercial deal it has with the sport's 11 teams says the calendar cannot drop below 22 races -- the cancellation of Qatar and Abu Dhabi, with no Imola race back-up, would make the final number 21.

Formula 1 appears to be confident there will not be a big issue in that scenario given the hosting fee paid by the Bahrain Grand Prix to rearrange their race in Malaysia in October.

The sport still intends to race in the Middle East and has been in constant communication with governments in both countries to monitor the situation. The Qatar circuit that is set to be used by F1 next month hosts MotoGP this weekend.

A majority of MotoGP's riders signed a letter ahead of the event expressing their wish not to race, but the championship threatened any riders who boycotted with sporting penalties.

Yamaha has pulled out of the event having found no reason to change its travel policy towards the Middle East. When asked about the MotoGP situation, Mercedes boss Toto Wolff said he would be fine with F1 adopting a similar approach.

"Stefano [Domenicali, F1 boss] and Mohammed [Ben Sulayem, FIA president] have been pretty clear about the situation that Formula 1 follows what the international guidelines are, whether there are travel restrictions, airlines not flying, any warnings in the region, the kind of feedback that local governments are making," Wolff said. "So not only the promoters, but what the local governments are making. And this is what you need to rely on, in my opinion, and I'm fully with that.

"I think that if [MotoGP] riders stand up, who know nothing geopolitically about what's going on, but have an audience that listens, I think that is something that creates media value. But I would have done the same as MotoGP management has done. You want to ride or drive, go. If you don't want to, don't go. It's as simple as that, and everybody can take their personal decisions on that, and I respect that.

"Of course, you've got to be wary of what's happening in the next few days, few weeks, and Stefano has his finger on the pulse to monitor that. If things were to get more dangerous and we would get that feedback, then he's going to be the first one, together with Mohammed, to protect the people that were meant to travel. So that's why I'm following their guidance."

When Wolff was asked what his policy would be on Mercedes team members expressing a desire to miss the Middle East races, he downplayed how concerned his staff are about going.

"From what I'm hearing internally, it hasn't been raised," he added. "It hasn't been a topic. But also there, if someone feels they don't feel comfortable, he or she doesn't feel comfortable travelling, then it's something that I would always respect. And maybe that's an opportunity to give somebody else a chance. It wouldn't change anything for the relationship. I've always respected that some people didn't want to go to certain Grands Prix, and that's how I see it at the moment."

stories.headline: Who should win 2026 MLS awards: Messi for MVP? Sullivan best young player?
stories.summary: With the MLS regular season coming to an end this weekend, ESPN asked its analysts to make their choices for the league's year-end awards.
stories.byline: Jeff Carlisle and Cesar Hernandez and Lizzy Becherano
stories.body:
The 2026 MLS regular season comes to a close Saturday. So much has happened in the 259 days since the campaign began -- there was a whole FIFA World Cup in the middle of the year, remember that? -- and that unpredictability has delivered some unexpected candidates for the league's year-end awards.

Back in February, who among us thought that then-16-year-old Cavan Sullivan would play at an MVP level? Who knew that Antoine Griezmann would hit the ground running upon his long-awaited arrival in North America? Who knew that former United States interim manager B.J. Callaghan would lead Nashville SC to the Supporters' Shield?

Although, there is always one constant you can count on: Lionel Messi playing at a level that no one has ever seen before in MLS.

So, on the eve of the season's final matchday, ESPN asked its writers: Who are you picking for this year's awards? Jeff Carlisle, Cesar Hernandez and Lizzy Becherano make their selections for coach of the year, young player of the year, newcomer of the year and Landon Donovan MVP.

Coach of the year

B.J. Callaghan, Nashville SC: This category is probably the toughest to pick. The midseason turnaround put in by the Philadelphia Union's interim manager Ryan Richter has been stunning. St. Louis City's Yoann Damet has accelerated the club's turnaround, with a 19-game unbeaten streak, and a U.S. Open Cup title, although they've faded of late.

Bruce Arena has gotten the San Jose Earthquakes back to the playoffs in his second season, no small feat given the club's usual level of ineptitude. The excellent season put in by FC Dallas' Eric Quill has flown under the radar. And then there's Callaghan, who now has a major trophy on his résumé with this year's Supporters' Shield triumph.

This probably comes down to a two-man race between Richter and Callaghan. My nod goes to Callaghan given Nashville is on the cusp of a record-setting points haul this season. -- Carlisle

Marko Mitrovic, New England Revolution: Expectations were modest, at best, for the Revs as they headed into 2026 under Mitrovic. Following a 2025 season that saw them once again miss out on the playoffs thanks to their 11th-place finish in the Eastern Conference, this year was anticipated to be more of a rebuild than anything else.

Instead, what followed was plenty of defensive solidity that propelled them up to their fourth place in the Supporters' Shield standings. In attacking support, Mitrovic has also gotten the best out of Carles Gil, who leads the team in goal contributions with 25. After a few years coaching within the U.S. youth international structure, Mitrovic is now thriving at the senior level. -- Hernandez

B.J. Callaghan, Nashville SC: Callaghan undoubtedly deserves this trophy for the incredible work he's done with Nashville. The team lifted the Supporters' Shield and tied Miami's MLS regular-season points record with one game left in the campaign. He's elevated the club since joining in 2024, taking a good roster to a trophy-winning club.

"B.J. is an excellent coach, very talented coach," said Hany Mukhtar. "What impresses me most is that he's always willing to improve -- constantly willing to improve the team, constantly willing to adjust and make players better and better and better. And that is, I think, the culture at this club." -- Becherano

Young player of the year

Cavan Sullivan, Philadelphia Union: I would be shocked if my colleagues selected anybody else. Once only on the radar of American soccer nerds, Sullivan has rapidly transitioned from teenage prospect to a genuine elite MLS player in 2026.

What's especially exciting about the 17-year-old is that he's not only shining on the stats sheet with his goals and playmaking, but also showing off a compelling level of tenacity and fight for a player who is still technically a kid. He's a joy to watch, and it's only a matter of time before the rest of the world learns about the creative yet daring attack-minded player and future U.S. men's national team star. -- Hernandez

Julian Hall, Red Bull New York: This is a tough award to give with so much rising talent between Sullivan, Hall and Justin Ellis, but I have the Red Bull New York striker just narrowly edging out the others. He's developed steadily over the years, really breaking out this season under head coach Michael Bradley.

Hall has 13 goals and five assists in 31 games, becoming an integral part of the Red Bull roster. Hall also became the youngest player in MLS history to record a hat trick, doing so at 18 years and 50 days. He has so much potential to tap into yet, but he's already showing signs of stardom. -- Becherano

Cavan Sullivan, Philadelphia Union: The amount of attention attached to Sullivan's arrival in MLS as a 14-year-old would have sunk just about any player in the league at the same age. Two years on, he's grown to the point that he's begun exceeding the hype.

His six goals and ten assists in league play since the World Cup break have played a huge part in the Union's second-half revival, in which they rose from rock bottom of the league-wide standings to clinching a playoff spot. The only question heading into Decision Day is which team Philadelphia will play in the postseason. Even better, Sullivan has done it with a style that has generated a tidal wave of excitement over just how much he'll grow in the coming years. -- Carlisle

Newcomer of the year

Antoine Griezmann, Orlando City SC: Many questioned what version of Griezmann would arrive in Orlando after years of wanting to play in the U.S., but he quickly proved that he came to MLS to compete. Although he signed in March, he didn't join the team until July following the end of the LaLiga season. It took him little time to adjust, scoring just 48 minutes into his debut.

Since then, Griezmann has gone on to record 14 goals and eight assists in just 17 games. His contributions propelled Orlando from 12th place, sitting outside the playoffs upon his arrival, to clinching a place in the 2026 postseason. -- Becherano

Antoine Griezmann, Orlando City SC: This award looks to be a two-horse race. Do you go with the season-long excellence of the Houston Dynamo's Guilherme, and his 16 goals and 10 assists? Or do you opt for the second-half supernova that was Griezmann, with his 14 goals and eight assists?

Both players have vastly outperformed their xG+xA, with Guilherme by almost 13 goal contributions while Griezmann has nine more than expected, but it's hard to look past the fact that the France World Cup winner's numbers have come in about 1,000 fewer minutes. Orlando has also resurrected its playoff chances with Griezmann in the lineup, clinching a spot on Sunday. Those last two factors mean that Griezmann just edges out Guilherme for the award. -- Carlisle

Guilherme, Houston Dynamo: Some players need weeks, if not months, to adjust to MLS. Guilherme needed 66 minutes. Scoring in the second half of his debut match for Houston in February, the Brazilian then doubled the mark with a game winner that cemented a brace in his first-ever MLS game -- which foreshadowed what would eventually follow.

Since then, the 31-year-old has continued to be highly efficient with 16 goals and 10 assists across his 30 appearances. Although things have slowed down for a Houston side that have just one win in their past nine, they could still become dark horses in the playoffs if they have a healthy and fit Guilherme in the XI. -- Hernandez

Landon Donovan MVP

Lionel Messi, Inter Miami: Is there really any other choice? Numbers-wise, the Argentina World Cup winner has practically lapped the field with 26 goals and 16 assists, and Miami has done well enough as a team to make Messi's contributions vital.

To be clear, other players had outstanding seasons. There remains a chance that the best player on the best team, that being Nashville SC's Hany Mukhtar, will get some votes, but his 17 goals and eight assists don't stack up to Messi. Neither do the 14 goals and 17 assists that Evander put up for an inconsistent FC Cincinnati side. Had Griezmann been with the club for a whole season, he might have threatened Messi for MVP supremacy. But as it stands, Messi is the clear choice. -- Carlisle

Lionel Messi, Inter Miami: Surprise, surprise. Sure, there are plenty who will justifiably wonder if this is simply just a popularity vote when he once again wins this award, but the numbers don't lie.

Messi leads the league in goals, goal contributions and xA. Diving into American Soccer Analysis' Goals Added metric, which "measures a player's total on-ball contribution in attack and defense," the Argentine superstar is head and shoulders above every other player in MLS with a tally of 14.06. For reference, at second place is San Jose Earthquakes forward Preston Judd, with a tally of 4.37. No matter the fact that he'll turn 40 next year, Messi continues to be the most dominant figure in MLS. -- Hernandez

Lionel Messi, Inter Miami: For a third consecutive season, Messi deserves the MVP award. He's recorded 26 goals and 16 assists in 30 games, carrying Inter Miami to second in the Eastern Conference, the Campeones Cup win over Cruz Azul and yet another Concacaf Champions Cup qualification.

Beyond the goals and assists, Messi's vision and IQ transform Inter Miami. The Herons struggled with consistency this season, playing under three coaches in the span of one campaign, but despite the constant chopping and changing, Messi remained the only positive constant. MLS may just have to change the name of the award given that Landon Donovan only won it twice. -- Becherano

stories.headline: Does Man United's coach matter? Could Jurgen Klopp reach Premier League glory at Old Trafford?
stories.summary: If Manchester United hired an all-time great like Jurgen Klopp, would they have won the Premier League? Let's find out!
stories.body:
Right around this time every year, you can start to feel it. The air gets a little crisper. The shadows get a little colder. The days get shorter. The tree colors start to pop. You start wearing sweaters. Pumpkins appear in places where they do and do not belong.

Everyone and everything starts to shift, just slightly, in preparation for what's about to happen. The cycles of nature can be fickle and unpredictable, so the date is never exactly the same, and some years come and go without anything at all. But most years, it does.

Our tiny little rituals prime us to anticipate the inevitable, oncoming shift: that moment when Manchester United fire their manager and convince themselves that the new guy is finally going to be the one who fixes everything.

Ruben Amorim lost his job last January. Erik ten Hag was fired two years ago, right before Halloween. Ole Gunnar Solskjaer got the boot just a couple of days before Thanksgiving. And Jose Mourinho was relieved of his duties a little over a week before Christmas.

Now that we've once again entered the season of sacking, Michael Carrick seems like he will inevitably become the latest victim.

Man United are clear of the relegation zone on goal differential alone. If history is any indication, their comeback against AS Roma in the Champions League will end up being meaningless. Before Tuesday's win, Carrick appeared to be on the verge of tears at the end of every match.

This is the 14th season since Manchester United last won the Premier League. And whoever replaces Carrick will be the ninth coach to try to do something that no other United manager since has done: just, simply, meet the expectations at one of the richest sports teams on the planet for more than a single season in a row.

But given how many different coaches have now failed since Sir Alex Ferguson left the club, it makes you wonder: Could anyone have been successful at Manchester United?

What is a great manager worth?

Arsenal won the Premier League last season with 85 points.

If we lived in a world where there were no subs and everyone on the field contributed exactly evenly to their team's success, then all 11 Arsenal players would have contributed about 8 points (7.7, to be slightly more exact) of value last season.

Except, the alternative to each player isn't just zero points. If you removed Bukayo Saka from the lineup, you wouldn't have to play a man down. No, you'd get to put another player out there who would also contribute to winning to some degree.

So, let's look at the relegation-level cutoff. West Ham were relegated with 39 points. Using the same framework, we'd say that all of their players were worth a little over 3.5 points across the season. We could then say that the average Arsenal player provided 5 more points of value than a relegation-level player.

This, of course, isn't exactly how it works: Some players are better than others, some positions are more valuable than others, and almost nobody plays 100% of the minutes. Goalkeeper David Raya played 97.3% of the league minutes last season, and Declan Rice led all outfield Gunners with 90.5% of minutes played.

But it all still gives us a nice benchmark. The best players on the best teams in the world are probably worth around 7 points more than your average relegation-level player. The truly generational superstars? You could probably bump that number up to 10 points if you wanted to.

But what about the manager? Rather than litigating the whole "managers don't matter" conversation for the 1,000th time on this website, we're just going to go with the logic put forth by Liverpool's former director of research, Ian Graham, in his book, "How to Win the Premier League": "[About] the same value as a good player brings. This is in line with manager salaries -- the best managers are paid a similar wage to the best players."

Who, then, was the best manager that Manchester United could've hired at any point over the past 14 seasons?

Most soccer-watchers would agree that there are two potential answers: Pep Guardiola or Jurgen Klopp. And most analyses would agree.

A 2025 study from the Sloan Sports Analytics conference looked at team performances from 2017 through 2024 across Europe's Big Five top leagues. The study awarded or penalized the manager for how much a team's performance level exceeded or undershot expectations based on the talent of the roster. Klopp and Guardiola topped the list -- with a significant gap between themselves and the next tier of coaches.

Given the 114 guilty charges against Manchester City under Guardiola, though, I think we have to go with Klopp. While Guardiola's influence on how the sport is played is undeniable, we now have to look on his Man City tenure skeptically. We know how much they outperformed what we were told they spent, but it would be foolish to blindly accept those numbers and attribute the gap purely to the Guardiola effect.

With Klopp, though, we know that he turned two clubs that were not even the richest clubs in their own leagues into two of the best teams in the world. And we know that he maintained those levels -- at both clubs -- for many seasons in a row. On top of that, both Borussia Dortmund and now Liverpool seem to have gotten worse after he left each job.

The job of the manager, simply, is to make his team better than the talent his club can afford to acquire and then to keep that improvement going even as the roster turns over. At the highest level of the sport, Klopp was better at that than any of his peers.

Could the best manager in the world save Manchester United?

What, then, might've happened if Manchester United somehow managed to hire Jurgen Klopp back in 2013 instead of David Moyes?

There are, of course, all kinds of ripple effects we could tease out -- what it would've done to German soccer, where Liverpool would've ended up, how Mohamed Salah's career would've played out, and on and on.

But I just want to focus on what it would've meant for Manchester United. We know that Liverpool benefitted from hiring Jurgen Klopp. But we also know that Jurgen Klopp benefitted from working for a club that did things like convincing him to sign Mohamed Salah instead of Julian Brandt.

Liverpool's cutting-edge front office didn't turn the club into the best team in the world, and neither did Klopp. No, it was the combo of the two that did it.

We could say similarly about Borussia Dortmund. At the time, Dortmund were one of the leaders in both youth development and identifying young stars. This meant that Klopp got the ideal kinds of talent, energetic youngsters to play his high-pressing style: Robert Lewandowski, Mats Hummels, Marco Reus, and Ilkay Gündogan -- just to name a few.

What we know about Manchester United, broadly, is that the club is an abject disaster. In terms of doing things that increase their chances of winning games, they are pretty much as bad as it gets. Since 2013, United have finished at or higher in the table than their relative Premier League revenue ranking once -- and that was last season.

While we could employ some magical thinking and convince ourselves that the only problem here is that the club can't hire the right coach, that's obviously not true. If it were, it would mean that the club that keeps firing its coaches just so happens to be doing all of the other things right.

No, the failure to find a successful long-term coach is a symptom of all of the other issues that plague the club. They've so badly underperformed their resources for over a decade; we can confidently say there is something deeply wrong with the way Manchester United tries to build its soccer teams.

So, if Klopp were the Man United coach, he wouldn't have fixed all of those problems. No, he would've had to work within that dysfunctional environment. He would've, in other words, ended up with Brandt instead of Salah -- many times over.

But let's sketch out the absolute best-case scenario for this hypothetical. Let's say that United have continued to hire "relegation-quality" managers. And let's say that Klopp's value is equivalent not just to the best player on a title team but to a true, once-in-a-generation superstar.

Neither of those things is true -- United aren't constantly hiring genuinely bad coaches, and Klopp himself would tell you that he's not worth the same as Lionel Messi -- but stretching the effect out to the extreme helps make the point.

Plus, by applying a Messi-like effect every year, we're canceling out some of the other problems with this exercise: not addressing the Manchester City situation, not subtracting points from other teams, not accounting for the increased spending power from an increased performance level, and so on.

If Klopp could've added 10 points to every Manchester United season, here's how things would've changed:

On average, United would've ended up with 76 points per season instead of 66, and their average finishing position would've been 3.8 instead of 5.3.

So, of course: things would be better if Manchester United had employed the best manager of the modern era for the last decade-plus. In this scenario, they would've finished in the top four 10 times, rather than six. Perhaps there would've been a deep Champions League run at a club that reached three finals in four seasons from 2008 to 2011 and hasn't been beyond the quarterfinals since.

But even if we granted Manchester United 13 straight seasons of consistent, transformative, incomparable, once-in-a-generation managerial performance, the team would still find itself right where it sits today: with no Premier League titles since Sir Alex Ferguson left the club.

stories.headline: The Philippine legend who keeps Jonny Parsons going
stories.summary: Philippine hero Lapu-Lapu defeated Ferdinand Magellan at the Battle of Mactan in 1521, and the story carries a personal meaning for Jonny Parsons that he takes with him every time he steps into the Octagon.
stories.body:
More than 500 years after Lapu-Lapu defeated Ferdinand Magellan at the Battle of Mactan, his legacy continues to inspire generations of Filipinos.

For UFC fighter Jonny Parsons, that story carries a personal meaning that he takes with him every time he steps into the Octagon.

Parsons, a Filipino-American whose mother is from Cebu, learned about the legendary warrior only in 2020, well into his mixed martial arts career. But once he discovered Lapu-Lapu's story, he found a connection to the resilience and spirit that have become part of his identity as a fighter.

"I have the warrior spirit," Parsons told ESPN. "My mom is from Cebu, so I have that Lapu-Lapu fighting spirit in me.

"It's definitely about resilience and holding it down for your people."

On April 27, 1521, Lapu-Lapu led native warriors against Magellan's forces at the Battle of Mactan in the Visayan islands of the Philippines. Using their knowledge of the terrain, the defenders overcame the Portuguese explorer's armed expedition and killed Magellan, disrupting Portugal's efforts to establish control over the islands.

Lapu-Lapu's victory remains a defining moment in Philippine history. He is celebrated as a symbol of Filipino resistance, courage and independence.

Parsons will carry that same resolve into his next challenge. The 35-year-old is set to face José Souza in a welterweight bout at UFC Fight Night: Cortes-Acosta vs. Walker.

"It's just a great story about overcoming the odds," Parsons said.

"They won that battle against Magellan, and in [Lapu-Lapu's] lifetime, the Philippines wasn't conquered. It wasn't until years after he was gone that they were conquered.

"I definitely want to say that my fighting spirit comes from that side of the family."

Parsons will have his own odds to overcome against Souza, as the Brazilian stands 6-foot-3 and holds a 10-inch reach advantage over the 5-foot-9 Parsons.

Souza, 24, carries a 9-1 professional record and is 1-0 in the UFC. On the other hand, Parsons owns a 9-3 record, including a 1-0 mark in the UFC.

The Filipino-American is returning from a layoff of 40 months after persistent hip flexor and groin injuries disrupted his training and kept him away from competition.

Still, he believes he has the tools to deal with the physical disadvantage and make a statement in his return.

"I'm no stranger to fighting a taller, longer opponent," he said.

"I think I have all the tools and weapons to defeat this guy [Souza].

"It just means that everyone's going to be able to see the best Jonny Parsons so far. But not the best ever, because I'm still getting better."

The extended break did not mean stepping away from the sport. Parsons, who is also now a mixed martial arts coach, kept training, shifting his focus to building strength, improving his conditioning, and addressing the physical issues that had held him back.

"This whole time that I've been off, I've been training," he told ESPN.

"I've been focusing on my strength and conditioning to help mend injuries and certain problem areas that were giving me issues during training.

"So I would say right now, I'm the healthiest and strongest I've ever been."

The experience also forced Parsons to rethink how he prepares for fights.

Rather than pushing through every session, he learned to treat recovery as seriously as training to develop a more disciplined approach to keeping his body healthy.

"I put a very heavy emphasis on my strength and conditioning training here in Vegas at the Performance Institute," he said.

"I also put much more effort into my recovery. Sometimes recovery, well, actually all the time, recovery is not just laying in bed and resting.

"Recovery is stretching. Recovery is a cold plunge, a sauna and walking. So I've really developed a much smarter training regimen that has allowed me to train at a very high level while avoiding all types of injuries."

Parsons is ready to show what that patience and discipline have produced.

"I'm very calm when I go into fights, and I'm very peaceful. I know I fight the best when I'm at peace. And it's very easy for me now to find that peace."

stories.headline: Relative obscurity to pick 1 buzz: WA's Heath Mellody is the ultimate bolter
stories.summary: Heath Mellody was a relatively unknown prospect earlier in the year. But then the National Championships came around, and the Larke Medallist suddenly has open pool pick 1 buzz, writes Jasper Chellappah.
stories.body:
Heath Mellody was sporting a new look at the AFL Draft combine. Usually standing out with the long, curly locks flying through the midfield, the Hale School graduate was hard to recognise with a buzzed dome.

He and schoolmates in Perth shaved their hair in the name of brain cancer research to venerate a Hale student.

Ryan Murphy passed away in early 2023 from glioblastoma, an incurable brain tumour. Mellody and his friends have been paying tribute ever since, with all proceeds being donated to the Harry Perkins Institute of Medical Research.

It's become a tradition at a school that has meant so much to Mellody. He opted to play his state-based footy with Hale in the PSA over the Claremont Colts.

From representing Western Australia at the national championships to running out on Optus Stadium for the WAFL Grand Final, his stocks have just kept on rising.

"School, academy, state and WAFL, it's just been so good," Mellody told ESPN.

"I love playing PSA footy with all my schoolmates. I sort of realised it'd probably be my last time playing with them.

"I didn't want to take it for granted, just tried playing like I usually would, preparing the same for any game. I loved every game and just had so much fun playing with my mates."

With no vision of the competition and no data being captured by Champion Data it kept Mellody hidden through the first portion of the season. That all changed at the National Champs.

"I was playing predominantly halfback and in the trial games I was having more of a split, and I was always playing a bit better in the midfield.

"I was always planning on playing midfield for parts of the first two games but that just didn't eventuate. But just before halftime of the Marvel game (against Vic Country) I got moved into the middle.

"I definitely prefer playing inside and it was just super fun going in there. We sort of mixed it up a bit in there and it gave us a bit more intent, bit more run and carry which in the end really helped.

WA was trailing Vic Country 38-10 before his move on-ball. They then piled on nine goals to three in the second half to storm over the top in front of every recruiter in the country.

Mellody was the firestarter. He won hard balls through the middle and used his trademark dash to put speed on the ball in transition. His hands were lightning under pressure and he had some special moments forward of centre that will be ingrained in those recruiters' minds.

The then-17-year-old finished with 33 disposals in the biggest 'pick me' game of the year.

He ended his epic champs with the Larke Medal around his neck as the best performed player at the carnival, joining the likes of Will Ashcroft, Sam Walsh and Christian Petracca by winning the award.

In truth, Mellody has been a prospect in demand since blitzing the colts grand final last season as a bottom-ager when he collected 25 touches and kicked a beautiful goal breaking the paint of 50 in a Claremont triumph.

"I loved playing Claremont colts last year. Getting connection with Charlie Banfield and Cody Curtin, playing AFL now, and going up against Toby Whan and Fred Rodriguez on Optus.

"That was so much fun and playing well in that finals series gave me a lot of confidence to go out and perform well this year."

That ended up being his final game of colts footy for Claremont because he was immediately called up to the senior team for a finals run this year. The Tigers surged from the middle of the ladder to make an unlikely grand final against a Peel side loaded with Fremantle talent.

Their best player in that grand final run was a teenager that missed his debut phone call because he was in second period at school.

"Ash [Prescott], the coach, gave me a ring while I was at school so I didn't actually pick it up. He called during the first couple periods... The head of sport at Hale told me to go get my phone and give him a call back!

"I went and did that and he was like 'Yeah, you're playing this week'."

Mellody's run at league level included a best on ground performance against a West Coast reserves midfield boasting the likes of Elijah Hewett, Fin Macrae and Harry Schoenberg. He took them to task with 34 disposals and a goal as Claremont rolled into finals.

"The biggest challenge was just working around the physicality of it. Obviously I'm a little bit smaller so it's going to be hard for me to body up so just working around that, getting off body, getting on the move a bit.

"The transition to the midfield made it a lot more comfortable for me at the level."

Mellody is now on the precipice of the top five, and has genuine pick 1 buzz. He's the most in-demand WA prospect since Luke Jackson, and West Coast is right in the mix at pick 3.

Mellody's beautiful kicking action and insatiable appetite to run and deliver is ideal for the modern game. He takes the ball from inside to out with leg drive that's reminiscent of Bailey Smith, though prides himself on his ball use going inside 50 and can pull off miraculous kicks when given space.

It may well be the Eagles who call Mellody's name, but the Bombers or Tigers will have first call on the unflappable teenager.

"I don't really have a preference to be honest. I'd just love to go anywhere, whether that be staying home or going interstate. I feel like it would be super cool and a great experience going anywhere... I've got a lot of support around Australia so I'll be able to manage if I were to move."

stories.headline: NRL transfer whispers: Manly shut down Paseka enquiry, Cowboys keen on Savage
stories.summary: The NRL season may be over, but the player market is heating up as we move beyond November 1. Isaac Issa has news on Bradman Best's future and which clubs might be lining up a play for Sam Walker.
stories.body:
The NRL season may be over, but the player market is heating up as we move beyond November 1, with clubs beginning to shape their rosters for 2027 and beyond.

From player movement to changes behind the scenes, ESPN NRL Insider Isaac Issa has the latest whispers from around the competition.

Warriors secure Seve homecoming

The Warriors are set to sign emerging centre Kingston Seve on a two-year deal after Newcastle granted him a release to return home to New Zealand.

ESPN understands Seve sought the release to make the move home, with the Warriors securing the promising outside back.

Seve featured in Newcastle's SG Ball and Jersey Flegg sides this season and represented Queensland in the under-19 State of Origin clash.

He will now continue his development with the Warriors as he works towards an NRL debut.

Sharks move to extend young star

Cronulla have tabled an offer to Liam Ison as they look to retain the young fullback beyond 2027.

ESPN understands the Sharks view Ison as part of their long-term plans and have moved to extend his stay.

The 21-year-old is contracted until the end of 2027, having signed an extension following a breakthrough 2024 season when he made his NRL debut and helped Newtown claim the NSW Cup premiership.

Ison's progress was interrupted by a ruptured ACL early in 2025, which ruled him out for the remainder of that season.

Cronulla's latest offer underlines their continued faith in his future.

Eels win race for Schiller

Parramatta have won the race for James Schiller, with ESPN understanding the outside back has agreed to terms on a two-year deal from 2027.

Multiple clubs, including the Wests Tigers, had shown interest in securing Schiller's services, but the Eels have moved to bolster their outside-back stocks.

Manly shut down Paseka enquiry
Manly have knocked back an enquiry from Canberra about Taniela Paseka's availability, with the Sea Eagles unwilling to release the prop.

ESPN understands the Raiders initiated the enquiry, contrary to reports Paseka had been shopped to the club.

While Manly are looking to move on Luke Brooks and Ethan Bullemor as they reshape their roster, Paseka is a player they want to retain.

The front-rower remains contracted to the Sea Eagles until the end of 2029.

Ricky Stuart has since publicly denied Canberra are pursuing Paseka.

Cowboys among clubs eyeing Savage

North Queensland are among the clubs showing interest in Canberra winger Xavier Savage, as rivals assess their recruitment options for 2028.

ESPN understands the Cowboys and a Sydney-based club are keeping tabs on the speedster, who is contracted to the Raiders until the end of 2027 and became eligible to negotiate with rivals on November 1.

Savage scored 13 tries in 19 NRL appearances for Canberra this season.

Bryenton begins Tigers chapter

David Bryenton will begin full-time training with the Wests Tigers on Wednesday, with ESPN understanding the recruit features in Benji Marshall's long-term plans.

Having first reported his signing last month, ESPN can reveal Bryenton's mutually agreed release from the Bulldogs has now been finalised, clearing the way for him to join Marshall's squad for pre-season.

Dolphins win race for Su'a

The Dolphins have won the race to retain Sebastian Su'a, with ESPN understanding the young forward has agreed to terms on a two-year extension that will keep him in Redcliffe until the end of 2029.

Several NRL clubs had identified Su'a as a potential recruitment target, but the Dolphins have moved to secure his future with the club.

Fa'alogo agrees to long-term Storm extension

Sua Fa'alogo has agreed to extend his stay at the Melbourne Storm through to the end of 2032, ESPN understands.

The agreement will keep the fullback in Melbourne for the next six seasons, securing a key figure in the Storm's long-term plans.

Fa'alogo's retention delivers a major boost for Melbourne ahead of the November 1 contracting window, with the club moving to lock down one of its most exciting talents.

Dolphins close in on Lemuelu extension, confident of keeping Farnworth

The Dolphins are closing in on a multi-year extension for Connelly Lemuelu as they also express confidence in retaining Herbie Farnworth.

ESPN understands Lemuelu is nearing an agreement to extend his stay despite interest from Canberra, Parramatta and Cronulla.

Securing the back-rower would deliver a retention boost for the Dolphins, with the length of the proposed deal yet to be confirmed.

The club is also understood to be confident it can retain Farnworth despite links to the Sydney Roosters.

While that confidence is yet to translate into a confirmed extension, keeping the English international alongside Lemuelu would help preserve key combinations on the Dolphins' left edge.

Eels edge ahead in Best race
Parramatta have emerged as the frontrunners to land Bradman Best, with multiple sources indicating the Newcastle centre is increasingly likely to join the Eels beyond 2027.

Best has been identified as a priority target for Parramatta, who are looking to bolster Jason Ryles' backline with an established representative star.

While a deal is yet to be confirmed, the Eels are understood to be in the box seat despite Newcastle's efforts to retain him with a lucrative extension.

Bulldogs unlikely to enter Walker race
Canterbury are unlikely to enter the race for Sam Walker, with the Bulldogs backing their existing halfback options ahead of the upcoming season.

Despite suggestions the club could emerge as a potential destination for Walker, it is understood Canterbury are taking a wait-and-see approach rather than preparing to launch a pursuit.

The Bulldogs' immediate focus remains on the internal battle for the No.7 jersey, with Mitch and Alex Conti set to compete for the role over the offseason.

Canterbury have not completely shut the door on a move should circumstances change, but their current position suggests they are unlikely to become an active contender for Walker's signature.

For now, the Bulldogs are content to watch how the situation unfolds.

stories.headline: Fantasy football Week 9 inactives: Who's in and who's out?
stories.summary: Updated inactives and analysis based on the latest reports and official announcements leading up to kickoff.
stories.body:
Whom should you start? Whom should you sit? To help you set your fantasy football lineups and avoid starting an offensive player who won't be in the lineup, we'll post fantasy-relevant updates and analysis here as NFL teams release their official inactives lists.

Official Sunday inactives should begin coming in approximately 90 minutes before the scheduled kickoff times: around 11:30 a.m. ET for the early games and 2:30 p.m. ET for the late-afternoon games.

Refresh often for the latest information.

Don't forget to check these out: Mike Clay's Playbook | Week 9 Buzz

Week 9 Rankings | Matchup rankings for Week 9

Biggest concerns ahead of Sunday
Players in Spain
No injuries of note
Players with early starts
Deshaun Watson, QB, Browns (concussion): Watson missed practice to start the week before upgrading to limited Friday. While he is listed as questionable for Week 9, Shedeur Sanders will start in his place. Sanders does add some value with his legs, having rushed for over 20 yards in five of eight games last season. However, he had just one game in which he threw for multiple TDs or more than 210 yards (both coming in the same game). Even in a favorable matchup against the Saints, Sanders is only for those in need in superflex leagues.

Harold Fannin Jr., TE, Browns (groin): Fannin was added to the injury report Thursday, before being removed Friday. He does not carry an injury designation and will play in Week 9. He is a strong play in fantasy this week. It's a favorable matchup against the Saints for Fannin, who averaged 14.6 fantasy PPG with Sanders last year (9.9 with other QBs) and is coming off two huge performances.

George Pickens, WR, Cowboys (hamstring): Pickens was limited all week at practice and the Cowboys are hopeful he will play, despite him being listed as questionable for Week 9. Even though he has not duplicated his success from last season, Pickens still needs to be started each week. If TE Jake Ferguson sits, it could mean some added targets his way. If Pickens were to sit, Ryan Flournoy would be a worthy streaming option.

Jake Ferguson, TE, Cowboys (ankle): Ferguson exited early in Week 8 and missed practice Wednesday and Thursday before returning in a limited fashion Friday. He is questionable heading into Week 9. Some replacement options are Greg Dulcich, Chig Okonkwo and T.J. Hockenson.

Amon-Ra St. Brown, WR, Lions (ribs): St. Brown has been limited at practice this week and is questionable for Week 9. If he plays for the Lions, he is a must-start fantasy option. If he sits, expect Jameson Williams and Sam LaPorta to get more volume. Both are already strong starts. Isaac TeSlaa becomes an upside streaming option for those in need of a deeper option.

Malik Nabers, WR, Giants (knee): Nabers popped up on the injury report Thursday, which normally isn't ideal. However, it seems to just be a rest day. He told reporters he was "good" after practice and returned Friday. He is not on the final injury report and will play in Week 9. He is a must-start in fantasy football.

Cam Skattebo, RB, Giants (hamstring): Skattebo has not practiced this week and is doubtful for Week 9. While it seems unlikely he plays, the Giants are not ruling it out. If he were to sit, Devin Singletary would be worth using as an RB2 or flex option. RB1s have averaged 18 fantasy PPG against the Eagles the past three weeks.

Breece Hall, RB, Jets (quad): Hall will play in Week 9. Braelon Allen has played great in Hall's absence, so expect him to have a larger role than he did previously. But Hall is still the Jets' RB1. The Chiefs are a tough matchup, so fantasy managers should temper expectations, but Hall is still in play as an RB2. As for Allen, managers should certainly hold him as he is one of the best backup RBs in the NFL. It's also possible that he has a large enough role to have stand-alone flex value.

Jordyn Tyson, WR, Saints (hamstring): The Saints' first-round pick practiced in a limited fashion this week and is questionable for Week 9. While it is exciting to potentially have Tyson back, fantasy managers should take a wait-and-see approach. Not only would it be his first regular-season NFL game, but the Browns are a tough defense. If he sits, it would mean more opportunities for Devaughn Vele. Also worth noting with the Saints is that Travis Etienne Jr. has not yet returned to practice.

Saquon Barkley, RB, Eagles (hamstring/back): Barkley returned to the practice field Thursday and is off the practice report, meaning he will play in Week 9. While he has been toughing it out through these injuries, it has led to him seeing limited usage. His big-play potential and touchdown upside keep him in the RB2 range. Some backs I would play over him are Jonah Coleman, Ollie Gordon II, Chase Brown, Josh Jacobs, Ashton Jeanty and Quinshon Judkins. However, unless you have enough of those backs to play over Barkley, start him.

-->

Players with late starts
Christian Watson, WR, Packers (rib): Watson has been limited at practice but does not carry an injury designation and will play in Week 9. He literally returned from the hospital and continued playing last week, so I would expect him to play this week. Watson is the WR3 entering Week 9. He is a must-start option.

Christian McCaffrey, RB, 49ers (hamstring): After sitting out Wednesday, McCaffrey was able to return to practice. He does not carry an injury designation for Week 9, meaning he will play. That means you start him in fantasy football.

Mike Evans, WR, 49ers (Achilles): Evans has not practiced this week and is unlikely to play in Week 9. The Niners will also likely be without Deebo Samuel. That leaves Christian Kirk and Demarcus Robinson, who is expected to return this week, as the top receivers for Brock Purdy. Both are deep league options. This ultimately means more targets for George Kittle and McCaffrey (if he plays).

Players on Sunday night
Emeka Egbuka, WR, Buccaneers (foot): Egbuka sat out Wednesday before returning to practice in full fashion Thursday. He is questionable for Week 9. Prior to being injured, Egbuka had been playing well, posting 17-plus fantasy points in each of his last two games. Baker Mayfield has just 64 passing yards the past two weeks combined (one was a weather game), but Egbuka is still worth playing as a WR3 with upside. Play him over Stefon Diggs, Jaylen Waddle, Makai Lemon and the Jets receivers.

Players on Monday night
DJ Moore, WR, Bills (shoulder): Moore has been limited this week, just as he has in past weeks, but he seems likely to play in Week 9. In the three full games he has played this season, he has a 29% target share, 42% air yard share and averaged 16.8 fantasy PPG. Even in a tough matchup, he is in play as a WR2. It is worth noting that Keon Coleman was limited and wearing the noncontact jersey at Bills practice.

Dalton Kincaid, TE, Bills (chest): Kincaid was limited to start the week before upgrading to full on Friday. Still, fantasy managers should look to avoid this matchup against the Vikings. Minnesota has allowed the fewest fantasy PPG and zero touchdowns to tight ends this season.

Ruled out before Sunday

Bam Knight, RB, Cardinals (concussion): Knight has not practiced this week and is out for Week 9. Tyler Allgeier should handle the bulk of work if Knight sits. Allgeier is coming off a huge performance, but he faces a much tougher matchup against the Seahawks. Seattle has allowed the sixth-fewest rushing yards per game to RBs. Allgeier is a volume flex option.

Jeremiyah Love, RB, Cardinals (ankle): Love suffered a high ankle sprain that is expected to hold him out four to five weeks. He has been placed on IR, meaning he will miss a minimum of four weeks. Tyler Allgeier is coming off his biggest game as a Cardinal and could once again see a heavy workload. Volume has him as a flex option. He does have a tough matchup, though, as the Seahawks allow the sixth-fewest rush yards per game to RBs.

Terrance Ferguson, TE, Rams (ankle): The Rams' TE was nearing a return from the IR and was expected to play in Week 9. However, he hurt his hamstring Friday and will now be out for Week 9. He is still worth stashing, as during his last healthy game he turned nine targets for six receptions, 54 yards and a touchdown. He could be the No. 2 target for the Rams moving forward. However, his availability, or lack thereof, is becoming an issue. Colby Parkinson (ribs) and Jordan Whittington (back) are both questionable for the Rams as well.

NBA Cup FAQ: Everything to know
What is the format?

NBA commissioner Adam Silver has had a longstanding fascination with European soccer. Establishing an in-season cup competition within the NBA schedule came from soccer leagues having both a regular-season title, won by the team with the most points over the full year, and a separate tournament (or, in some leagues, multiple tournaments) that runs concurrently with the league season.

In England, for example, there are the various divisions -- led by the Premier League -- and also the FA Cup competition. But unlike those European leagues, which play their cup competitions outside of their league schedules, the NBA Cup is built in to the regular-season slate.

The 30 NBA teams are split into six five-team groups -- three featuring Eastern Conference teams and three comprising Western Conference teams -- with each team then playing one game against the other four in its group. The winner of each group, plus the team with the best record among the non-group winners, advances to the knockout stage of the competition.

How will this impact the regular-season schedule and standings?

Typically, the NBA sends out a full 82-game schedule in mid-August. Now, the league sends out only 80 games and leaves a gap of roughly a week to fill in later, depending on how the group stage of the NBA Cup plays out.

The two teams from the East and West that lose in the quarterfinals will play their 82nd game against each other. Meanwhile, the 22 teams that fail to qualify for the knockout rounds will have their final two games scheduled -- one at home and one on the road against others eliminated in the group stage.

The teams that reach the NBA Cup final will actually play 83 games -- though the championship game won't count toward the standings or any statistical markers. The four teams that reach the semifinals will have completed their 82 games and won't need any other games added to their schedule.

Any team that makes it to the semifinals will have that game moved later in the schedule to avoid back-to-back games. The NBA made this change in an effort to avoid having empty days on the calendar while attempting to minimize back-to-backs for all teams as much as possible.

Where are the semifinals and final being played?

In a shift from previous tournaments, the quarterfinals and semifinals will be played at home sites. The Dec. 11 title game, meanwhile, will move from Las Vegas to the storied Hinkle Fieldhouse in Indianapolis. NBA commissioner Adam Silver previously said the league was searching for "storied college arenas" to play host to the Cup final. (No venue has been announced for 2027.)

Why does the NBA Cup include regular-season games?

Before its launch, one of the main questions surrounding the in-season tournament was why any team would be incentivized to compete in it. The NBA ensured teams will be motivated by making every game part of the season and, as in-conference matchups, potentially important to playoff tiebreakers. If this had been set up like the cup tournaments in European soccer, there would have been nothing stopping NBA teams from opting out by sitting their top players for extra rest.

Which teams make up the groups?

To create the groups, the NBA put the 15 teams in each conference into five pots, separated by their finish last season. Pot 1 included the teams that finished in the top three in the regular-season standings, Nos. 4-6 in the standings went into Pot 2, Nos. 7-9 into Pot 3, Nos. 10-12 into Pot 4 and Nos. 13-15 into Pot 5. As a result, the following groups were drawn:

Does one group stand out the most from the others?

East Group B is a monster.

All five teams -- defending NBA Cup and Finals champion New York, Philadelphia, Cleveland, Miami and Indiana -- are among the favorites to win the conference in 2026-27. The group stage will also feature reunion games for LeBron James, when the 76ers face the Cavs and Heat. And after guard Tyrese Haliburton missed the entire 2025-26 season while rehabbing a torn Achilles, the Pacers will be back among the East elite and hungry to reach the title game in Indianapolis.

What do players get for winning?

In 2023, the first year the tournament was held, the players on the winning team received $500,000 each and the runners-up got $200,000. The losing players of the semifinals each got $100,000, and those ousted in the quarterfinals got $50,000. Now, in each subsequent year, the prizes will be slightly higher, as a result of negotiated raises year over year to keep pace with increases in the salary cap and basketball-related income as part of the most recent collective bargaining agreement between the NBA and the National Basketball Players Association.

Will anyone earn individual honors for their play in NBA Cup games?

There will be an MVP award, as well as an all-tournament team.

Will this have any impact on the playoffs?

Not beyond the games counting in the regular-season standings (and toward tiebreakers). The only playoff impact comes from the wins and losses accrued throughout the tournament. Though there was debate among league insiders about guaranteeing a playoff berth for winning the tournament, ultimately that idea (or any other to further incentivize teams) was not enacted.

Why is it called the Emirates NBA Cup?

The league struck a sponsorship deal with Emirates, the Dubai-based airline, to sponsor the tournament after its initial run. The NBA said last year that it went with the most basic titles for both the tournament and its trophy -- the "in-season tournament" and "NBA Cup" -- as a way to introduce the concept to fans. However, using such nondescript names had another clear advantage: It gave the league a blank slate in case it sold the naming rights for the tournament and cup to a sponsor and avoided the complications that could arise by naming them after someone (for example, late NBA commissioner David Stern, one possibility that had been floated before the tournament was officially unveiled).
